clue.text: In these, some babies may suffer burns

definitions.text: In these, some babies may suffer burns

parts.words: In these, some babies may suffer burns
parts.note: the babies are bushbabies, small African primates, and the burns are those of wildfires in scrubland

explanation.surface: A grim warning about infants being scalded.
explanation.walkthrough: The babies are not human: bushbabies live in scrub country, which is where these blazes rage.
explanation.definitionFit: Wildfires sweeping through scrub and woodland can harm the animals living there, bushbabies among them.

clue.text: End of 24 down

parts.words: End of 24 down
parts.note: the clue points at the smoked object at 24 down; its remaining stub is what is meant

explanation.surface: A bare cross-reference to the end of another clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 24 down is CIGAR, and what is left when it is smoked is its stub.
explanation.definitionFit: The stub left after smoking a cheroot or cigarette is called by this name, as is the thick end of anything.

clue.text: Even gates get broken in a new town

indicators.note: gates that get broken are smashed apart, so their letters are rearranged along with 'Even'

parts.words: Even gates

explanation.surface: Vandals smashing the gates in a freshly built town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'get broken' tells you to rearrange EVEN GATES. Stevenage, in Hertfordshire, was the first of Britain's post-war 'new towns', planned settlements built from 1946.
explanation.definitionFit: Stevenage was designated in 1946 as the first of Britain's planned post-war towns.

clue.text: One of those that are game when happy

definitions.text: One of those that are game when happy

parts.words: One of those that are game when happy
parts.note: Happy Families is a card game where players collect sets of relatives such as Mr Bun the Baker and his wife and children

explanation.surface: A remark about people who are willing whenever they are in a good mood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'game' looks like 'willing', but it is the noun: Happy Families is a British children's card game of collecting sets of relatives.
explanation.definitionFit: In the card game Happy Families each set of four cards is a household of parents and children.

clue.text: Where to look for those on the run

definitions.text: Where to look for those on the run

parts.words: Where to look for those on the run
parts.note: reads like a hunt for fugitives, but the runners are horses or athletes competing

explanation.surface: A tip for the police on where to find escaped criminals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'those on the run' sounds like fugitives, but they are runners in contests of speed.
explanation.definitionFit: Contests of speed are where runners are found running.

clue.text: Singular gift to the defeated

parts.words: Singular gift to the defeated
parts.note: to 'give someone ...' is old slang for beating them; one of the pair is the singular

explanation.surface: An odd present handed to the losing side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Singular' looks like 'remarkable', but it asks for the singular of the plural in the idiom 'give them socks', meaning beat them thoroughly. One item is also a punch.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'give someone socks' means to thrash them, and in the singular the word is also slang for a hard blow.

clue.text: " My word!" as one might well say

annotationWithheld.why: " My word!" as one might well say (5): no parse found that gives MONAD from these words
annotationWithheld.clue: " My word!" as one might well say

clue.text: It isn't necessarily shown on a relief map

definitions.text: It isn't necessarily shown on a relief map

parts.words: It isn't necessarily shown on a relief map
parts.note: a relief map shows hills; this South African town is famous for its relief, the lifting of a siege in 1900

explanation.surface: A geography note about what contour maps leave off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'relief' means raised terrain on a map, but the Relief of Mafeking ended a 217-day siege in the Boer War and set off wild celebrations in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: This South African town was besieged by Boer forces until its relief in May 1900.

clue.text: It's no light matter when a thing goes awry

indicators.note: the thing that goes awry is knocked out of shape, so its letters are rearranged

parts.words: thing

explanation.surface: A warning that things going wrong is a serious business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goes awry' rearranges THING. 'No light matter' sounds like 'serious', but it means the hours of darkness.
explanation.definitionFit: The hours of darkness are the time with no daylight.

clue.text: Could he give us a lecture on foreign relations ?

definitions.text: Could he give us a lecture on foreign relations ?

parts.words: Could he give us a lecture on foreign relations ?
parts.note: a stern lecturer is called by this name, and the phrase also names a kinsman from the Netherlands

explanation.surface: A question about whether someone could speak on international affairs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'foreign relations' sounds like diplomacy, but it is literally a relative from abroad: the idiom names someone who gives a severe talking-to.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a person who criticises or lectures severely, and literally it is a Netherlander kinsman.

clue.text: Promise of warmth from the weather-man

indicators.note: the letters are taken out of the run of the compound word that follows

parts.words: weather-man

explanation.surface: A forecaster promising warmer days ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' lifts the letters straight out of 'weather-man', across the hyphen.
explanation.definitionFit: A therm is a unit of heat used to bill gas supplies, so it stands for warmth on order.

clue.text: Feathers fly in the main event

definitions.text: Feathers fly in the main event

parts.words: Feathers fly in the main event
parts.note: a 'main' is an old name for a match of fighting birds, where plumage really does fly

explanation.surface: A heated contest at the top of the bill gets everyone ruffled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'main event' reads as the headline bout, but a main is the cockpit term for a set match between gamebirds.
explanation.definitionFit: Two roosters set against each other shed plumage as they battle in a 'main'.

clue.text: With no visible means of support ?

definitions.text: With no visible means of support ?

parts.words: With no visible means of support ?
parts.note: reads like someone with no income, but the means of support are limbs to stand on

explanation.surface: A remark about someone apparently living on nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase usually describes an idler with no income; here it is a body or table lacking the limbs that hold it up. British slang also uses the word for very drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Something without limbs has nothing to stand on, no visible means of being held up.

clue.text: Outline by Boz

parts.words: Outline by Boz
parts.note: Boz was the early pen name of Charles Dickens, whose first book was a collection of short descriptive pieces

explanation.surface: A rough drawing attributed to an artist called Boz.
explanation.walkthrough: Dickens wrote as Boz in 'Sketches by Boz' (1836), so a short piece by him bears this name as well as meaning an outline.
explanation.definitionFit: A rough preliminary drawing is an outline; Dickens's early pieces were titled the same way.

clue.text: Hush! Start a round of golf — it's competitive

parts.words: Hush
parts.note: whist is an old exclamation calling for silence

parts.words: Start a round of golf
parts.note: the drive is the first long shot from the tee

explanation.surface: Someone shushes a golfer about to tee off in a competition.
explanation.walkthrough: A whist drive is a social evening of the card game whist with partners changing tables, popular in British church and village halls.
explanation.definitionFit: This social card evening is a contest in which players score points and move between tables for prizes.

clue.text: The right board for navigators

parts.words: The right board for navigators
parts.note: the right side of a ship is named with this word plus 'board', and navigators steer by it

explanation.surface: A remark about which plank or panel suits ship's navigators.
explanation.walkthrough: 'right board' is starboard, the right-hand side of a ship; the first part of that word is what navigators steer by in the night sky.
explanation.definitionFit: Navigators fix position by celestial bodies, and the right side of a ship is named after one with 'board' added.

clue.text: With her it grows, and to a considerable degree, maybe

definitions.meaning: add HER to the end of this word and you get a moorland plant, something that grows
a high temperature, many degrees on the thermometer

explanation.surface: A cryptic remark about something that thrives in a woman's company.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half is a puzzle in itself: the word plus HER makes HEATHER, a plant. 'Degree' is a step on the thermometer.
explanation.definitionFit: Hotness is measured in degrees, so a considerable number of them means warmth; adding a pronoun makes a moorland shrub.

clue.text: Something to look for at the end of the day

definitions.text: Something to look for at the end of the day

parts.words: Something to look for at the end of the day
parts.note: describes what appears low on the western horizon each evening

explanation.surface: A comforting thought about what to expect after a long day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At the end of the day' sounds like the cliché meaning 'ultimately', but here it is literally dusk.
explanation.definitionFit: At dusk the sky's light sinks below the western horizon, the sight one watches for in the evening.

clue.text: An old-world garden

parts.words: An old-world garden
parts.note: 'old-world' suggests quaint and traditional, but it is the very first garden of Genesis

explanation.surface: A description of a quaint, traditional garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'old-world' usually means charmingly quaint; here it is the garden of the world at its very beginning in Genesis.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis the first humans lived in this paradise garden at the dawn of the world.

clue.text: Pickwickian who blamed the salmon, not the wine

definitions.text: Pickwickian who blamed the salmon, not the wine

parts.words: Pickwickian who blamed the salmon, not the wine
parts.note: a poetic member of the Pickwick Club in Dickens who, being drunk, blamed his state on the salmon

explanation.surface: A diner insisting it was the fish, not the drink, that disagreed with him.
explanation.walkthrough: In Dickens's 'The Pickwick Papers' Augustus Snodgrass, drunk after the cricket dinner, says it was the salmon that upset him.
explanation.definitionFit: Augustus Snodgrass, the would-be poet of the Pickwick Club, puts his tipsiness down to the fish.

clue.text: Pets made to panic

indicators.note: the letters of the two words are made to panic, sent running in a new order

parts.words: Pets made

explanation.surface: Animals frightened into a sudden rush.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to panic' rearranges PETS MADE, and the whole clue describes a herd's frightened rush.
explanation.definitionFit: A sudden frightened rush of a herd of animals is exactly animals driven into panic.

clue.text: "Tray, Blanch, and ——, see, they bark at me" (Lear)

definitions.text: "Tray, Blanch, and ——, see, they bark at me" (Lear)

parts.words: "Tray, Blanch, and ——, see, they bark at me" (Lear)
parts.note: a quotation from King Lear with the third little dog's name missing

explanation.surface: Mad King Lear complains that even his little dogs bark at him.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed clue has a dash where the missing name goes: Lear says 'The little dogs and all, Tray, Blanch, and Sweetheart, see, they bark at me' (Act 3, Scene 6).
explanation.definitionFit: In the play this is the name of the third of the little dogs Lear imagines barking at him.

clue.text: He is rash, if hardy

parts.words: He is rash, if hardy
parts.note: join this word to 'hardy' and you get a compound adjective meaning rash or reckless

explanation.surface: A judgement on a bold man: hardy, perhaps, but reckless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hardy' is not an adjective about him but the second half of a compound: put the two together and you get foolhardy, meaning rash.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone reckless and silly is a simpleton, and the compound with 'hardy' means recklessly bold.

clue.text: The one needed to complete a pair of braces ?

definitions.text: The one needed to complete a pair of braces ?

parts.words: The one needed to complete a pair of braces ?
parts.note: a brace is two of something, so a pair of braces is a set of four; one short, you need the last of the set

explanation.surface: A question about the missing piece of clothing to hold up trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: Braces are British for trouser suspenders, but a brace is also a pair, so a pair of braces is four and the missing one is number four.
explanation.definitionFit: Two braces make four, so the last needed is the one in fourth position.

clue.text: What the Arabs do when they fold their tents ?

definitions.text: What the Arabs do when they fold their tents ?

parts.words: What the Arabs do when they fold their tents ?
parts.note: the line from Longfellow about folding tents and silently stealing away; to take down camp and leave

explanation.surface: A question about desert nomads packing up.
explanation.walkthrough: Longfellow's poem 'The Day Is Done' has cares that 'fold their tents, like the Arabs, And as silently steal away'. To strike camp is literally to break up a camp and leave.
explanation.definitionFit: To leave suddenly, originally to break up an encampment, which is what folding up tents amounts to.

clue.text: This one gets extremely hot and puffed

definitions.text: This one gets extremely hot and puffed

parts.words: This one gets extremely hot and puffed
parts.note: sounds like an exhausted runner, but it is a roll of tobacco leaf lit at the tip and drawn on

explanation.surface: An athlete getting overheated and out of breath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'puffed' suggests breathlessness, but it is smoked: its tip glows hot and the smoker puffs on it.
explanation.definitionFit: A roll of tobacco leaf burns at its tip and is puffed on by the smoker.

clue.text: Finished in front of the looking-glass literally ?

definitions.text: in front of the looking-glass literally ?
definitions.meaning: Lewis Carroll's Alice book title begins with this word, which stands right in front of 'the Looking-Glass'

explanation.surface: Someone finished primping before the mirror.
explanation.walkthrough: 'literally' points at the words of a title: Carroll's sequel is 'Through the Looking-Glass', so this word comes in front of 'the looking-glass'.
explanation.definitionFit: Done means finished; and in Carroll's title the word sits immediately before 'the Looking-Glass'.

clue.text: He takes steps to enjoy himself

definitions.text: He takes steps to enjoy himself

parts.words: He takes steps to enjoy himself
parts.note: 'takes steps' sounds like making arrangements, but here it is walking for pleasure

explanation.surface: A man arranging matters so he can have a good time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes steps' is an idiom for taking action, here read literally as walking for pleasure.
explanation.definitionFit: A rambler walks the countryside for pleasure, so his steps are his enjoyment.

clue.text: Ring Winnie up !

indicators.note: in a down clue 'up' means the word is written from the bottom upwards, so it is turned around

parts.words: Winnie
parts.note: Winnie-the-Pooh, A. A. Milne's bear, is called Pooh

explanation.surface: Someone told to phone Winnie and wake her up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns Winnie's other name, POOH, into OOHP read from the bottom, giving the hoop. 'Ring' looks like a telephone call.
explanation.definitionFit: A circular band of wood or metal is a ring shape, like a child's bowling toy.

clue.text: To draw this one should have the right approach

definitions.text: To draw this one should have the right approach

parts.words: To draw this one should have the right approach
parts.note: 'draw' plus this word forms a phrase meaning come closer

explanation.surface: Advice for an artist on how to set about a drawing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'draw' looks like sketching, but 'draw near' means to approach, so this word follows 'draw'.
explanation.definitionFit: Close at hand; 'draw' plus this word means to come closer, which is the approach.

clue.text: Where one might find oneself in a warm corner

definitions.text: Where one might find oneself in a warm corner

parts.words: Where one might find oneself in a warm corner
parts.note: describes a seat set into the recess beside an open hearth

explanation.surface: A cosy picture of someone tucked up somewhere snug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a warm corner' can mean in a tight spot, but here it is literal: a recess beside the fireplace.
explanation.definitionFit: A chimney corner, a recess beside a large open fire, is a warm nook to sit in.

clue.text: Charles gives sound advice on what to do with his work

indicators.note: the advice is a word that, said out loud, matches the novelist's surname

parts.words: advice on what to do with his work
parts.note: the advice to give a book is to peruse it

explanation.surface: A novelist named Charles tells people what to do with his books.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Reade (1814-84) wrote 'The Cloister and the Hearth'. The advice for his books is the instruction 'read', which is pronounced like his surname; 'gives sound' is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Reade was a Victorian novelist, so his first name points to his surname.

clue.text: Always short ? That is weird !

indicators.note: the poetic contraction drops a letter, so the word for always is cut down

parts.words: Always
parts.note: always means ever, here in its poetic shortened form e'er

parts.words: That is
parts.note: i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, Latin for that is

explanation.surface: A complaint about something always falling short, which seems uncanny.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' signals the poets' contraction E'ER, which loses the V from EVER; then IE follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Uncanny and weird are synonyms for strange in an unsettling way.

clue.text: Sharp cure for one on a spending spree, perhaps

indicators.note: the letters of the two opening words could perhaps be arranged another way, signalling a rearrangement

parts.words: Sharp cure

explanation.surface: A remedy for a shopaholic who keeps buying things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' asks for the letters of SHARP CURE to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone on a shopping spree is a buyer, one who acquires goods for money.
